> **What this case shows** — a walker is described at once by how the limbs *move*
> (kinematics) and by the forces under the foot (kinetics). Do the two modalities
> carry the same information? The **distance correlation** (Székely, Rizzo & Bakirov
> 2007) answers this *without assuming linearity*: it is zero **iff** two multivariate
> blocks are independent, and catches any dependence a Pearson or linear-canonical
> measure would miss. On real WBDS treadmill walking, the sagittal knee+ankle flexion
> angles and the antero-posterior+vertical GRF have **dCor = 0.72** (permutation
> **p = 0.001**) for one subject and **0.71–0.78** across all five (mean **0.74**) — a
> strong, significant, strikingly consistent coupling. The ecosystem's
> `distanceCorrelation` reproduces the canonical **`energy::dcor` to machine precision**
> (|diff| < **1e-13**), so the measure is *exact*, not approximate.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to ask whether two modalities are dependent: form two **time-aligned
blocks** (here kinematics vs kinetics) → call `distanceCorrelation(X, Y,
permutations = 999)` → read the **dCor** and its **permutation p** → (optionally) repeat
across subjects for robustness.
**Way of thinking** — dependence is not the same as *linear* correlation. Distance
correlation measures dependence of *any* shape and is **zero iff independent**, so a
near-zero dCor is real evidence of independence, and a large dCor certifies coupling
even when no single pair of channels correlates linearly.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioCrossModal::distanceCorrelation()` for the coefficient +
permutation test; the same package's `representationalSimilarity()`,
`multipleFactorAnalysis()`, `coupledNMF()` and `jive()` for the wider cross-modal
toolkit.
:::

## Proposition

On real WBDS treadmill walking, gait kinematics (knee+ankle flexion) and kinetics
(GRF) are statistically dependent: dCor = 0.7225 (permutation p = 0.001) for WBDS01
and 0.71–0.78 (mean 0.74) across five subjects, and `distanceCorrelation` equals the
canonical `energy::dcor` to machine precision.

## Question & goal

**The question is whether two modalities of the same movement carry shared
information — and how to measure that honestly.** Linear correlation can be fooled: two
signals can be strongly dependent yet have a Pearson correlation near zero. The
distance correlation removes that blind spot — it is zero *if and only if* the blocks
are independent. The goal is to (1) quantify the kinematics–kinetics coupling on real
data and (2) show the ecosystem's operator is the *exact* Székely statistic by matching
the reference `energy::dcor`.

## Challenge & approach

Kinematics and kinetics live in different units and dimensions, so a coupling measure
must compare *blocks*, not single channels, and must not assume a linear map. Distance
correlation does exactly this: it correlates the **pairwise-distance** structure of the
two blocks. We form the two aligned blocks, compute dCor with a 999-permutation test,
and cross-check every value against `energy::dcor`.

```
knee+ankle flexion angles ┐
                          ├─ distanceCorrelation(X, Y, permutations = 999) → dCor, p
AP+vertical GRF           ┘        (validated == energy::dcor, |diff| < 1e-13)
```

## Data

**WBDS — Fukuchi, Fukuchi & Duarte (2018), PeerJ** (figshare 5722711, CC-BY 4.0): five
subjects of treadmill walking. For each, two time-aligned blocks — sagittal **knee +
ankle flexion angles** (marker-derived, translation-invariant) and the **antero-posterior
+ vertical GRF** — down-sampled to 450 samples. Because it is *treadmill* walking the
markers oscillate about fixed positions (no forward drift that would inflate the
coupling). Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: for WBDS01, each point is a *pair* of gait samples — its kinematic distance (x) versus its kinetic distance (y); the positive trend is the dependence distance correlation captures (dCor = 0.72, p = 0.001). Right: the kinematics–kinetics distance correlation for all five subjects (0.71–0.78, mean 0.74) — strong and consistent.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* distance correlation asks whether pairs of moments that are far
apart in *kinematics* are also far apart in *kinetics*. The rising cloud on the left
says yes; the bars on the right say it holds for every subject.

| Quantity | This reproduction | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| dCor (WBDS01) | **0.7225** | `energy::dcor` = 0.7225 |
| \|op − energy::dcor\| | **< 1e-13** | 0 (exact statistic) |
| Permutation p (999 perm) | **0.001** | — |
| Mean dCor, 5 subjects | **0.7447** | — |
| Min dCor, 5 subjects | **0.7118** | — |

The op reproduces `energy::dcor` to machine precision, the coupling is strong and
significant, and it holds across every subject. Values trace to
[`artifacts/crossmodal_dcor_summary.csv`](artifacts/crossmodal_dcor_summary.csv) and
[`artifacts/crossmodal_dcor_by_subject.csv`](artifacts/crossmodal_dcor_by_subject.csv).

## Conclusion

Gait kinematics and kinetics are two views of one act of walking, and the distance
correlation certifies their coupling *without* assuming linearity — on real data,
across every subject, with an operator that is the exact Székely statistic. The
transferable takeaway: **to test whether two modalities share information, correlate
their distance structure — a near-zero dCor is genuine evidence of independence, and a
large one certifies coupling even when no single channel pair correlates.**

## Open questions

- Distance correlation here is a **whole-block, marginal** measure. A *partial* distance
  correlation would ask whether the coupling survives removing gait speed; a
  channel-resolved **dCor screen** would map *which* kinematic and kinetic degrees of
  freedom drive it; and applying the same operator to genuinely different modalities
  (**EEG↔EMG**, **EMG↔force**) would turn a validated coupling statistic into a
  cross-modal discovery tool. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| distance correlation + permutation test | `distanceCorrelation()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| representational similarity (RSA) | `representationalSimilarity()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| multiple factor analysis (blocks) | `multipleFactorAnalysis()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| shared vs modality-specific structure | `jive()` | PhysioCrossModal |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **Blocks, not channels** — pass the whole kinematic and kinetic matrices; dCor
  compares their joint distance structure, so you do not pre-select channels.
- **Permutations** — 999 gives a smallest p of 0.001; raise it if you need a finer tail.
- **Alignment** — the two blocks must share rows (the same time samples / observations);
  down-sample together so the pairing is preserved.
- **Interpretation** — dCor ∈ [0, 1]; **0 iff independent**. Unlike |Pearson|, a small
  value is meaningful evidence of independence.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCrossModal)

# X = kinematics (n × p), Y = kinetics (n × q), same n rows (aligned samples)
dc <- distanceCorrelation(X, Y, permutations = 999, seed = 1)
dc$dcor      # 0.7225  — strong cross-modal coupling
dc$p_value   # 0.001   — significant (999-permutation null)

# exact by construction: matches the canonical energy::dcor
stopifnot(abs(dc$dcor - energy::dcor(X, Y)) < 1e-9)
```
